conversationGoal: Invite the child to admit whether they'd pop it too.
english: Bubble wrap used to be wallpaper.
Imagine a whole wall of it.
I wouldn't look at it, though.
I'd just pop the whole thing.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess what a wooden mouse would feel like.
english: The first computer mouse was made of wood.
Not plastic. Wood.
I keep imagining what that would feel like.
Warm, probably. Or a bit rough.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine taking ketchup as medicine.
english: Ketchup used to be sold as medicine.
Imagine your doctor saying, "take a spoonful of ketchup."
I'd probably ask for a second dose.
Just to be safe.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to try finding another word like this.
english: Queue. Q-U-E-U-E.
Now just say "Q."
Same sound.
Bet you can't find another word like that.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to the idea of a painless brain.
english: Your brain can't feel pain.
No pain receptors in there at all.
So you could poke it and feel nothing.
I'm not going to try that, though.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine the inventor's real reaction.
english: Microwaves exist because a chocolate bar melted in someone's pocket.
His actual pocket.
I keep wondering what his face looked like.
Probably not "eureka."

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what job or title they'd want.
english: Ancient Egyptians gave cats an actual job.
Guarding food from mice.
And they treated them like they mattered.
I'd want a title, at least.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to wonder how well they'd guess their food in the dark.
english: Some restaurants in Japan serve food in complete darkness.
No lights at all.
You'd have to guess everything by taste.
I wonder if I'd get any of it right.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what their own vending machine would sell.
english: The very first vending machine was over 2,000 years old.
It sold holy water.
Not snacks. Holy water.
Mine would probably just sell socks.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to admit what mundane thing they'd want to watch.
english: The first webcam only existed to watch a coffee machine.
People just wanted to know if there was coffee left.
Honestly, I'd point mine at a fridge.
Just to check on the snacks.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to try saying the word themselves.
english: "Strengths" is the longest English word with only one vowel.
Say it slowly: strengths.
It barely even sounds like a word.
My mouth doesn't know what to do with it.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to having their heart in their head.
english: A shrimp's heart is in its head.
Not its chest. Its head.
Imagine if yours was up there too.
You'd hear your own heartbeat when you thought.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess what you can actually see from space.
english: You can't actually see the Great Wall from the Moon.
Everyone says you can. You can't.
So what can you see from up there, I wonder.
Probably just... blue.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say whether they'd still eat the cheese.
english: Some cheese is made with the same bacteria that's on human skin.
The same kind.
I don't know what to do with that information.
I'm still going to eat the cheese, though.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to admit whether they'd have watched the whole thing.
english: The longest tennis match ever lasted more than 11 hours.
Eleven hours of just... tennis.
I'd have fallen asleep by hour two.
Snacks would have to last the whole time, though.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine living with that clock.
english: The first alarm clock could only ring at 4 a.m.
Just that one time. Every day.
Didn't matter what time you needed to get up.
4 a.m. it is, apparently.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say who their best friend is.
english: Cows can have a best friend.
A real one. They even get upset when they're apart.
I wonder who mine would be.
Probably whoever shares their snacks.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to invent their own two-second song.
english: The shortest song ever released lasts about two seconds.
Two seconds. That's it.
I couldn't even finish saying "hello" in that time.
What would your two-second song be?

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what object they'd turn into a game.
english: The first Frisbees weren't Frisbees. They were cake tins.
Someone just threw one.
And then, apparently, they kept doing it.
I respect that kind of commitment.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to being treated with leeches today.
english: Doctors used to treat illness with leeches.
On purpose. As medicine.
Imagine your doctor handing you one today.
I'd ask for a second opinion.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to wonder who decided fashion should change.
english: High heels were first worn mostly by men.
Not women. Men.
I wonder when that changed.
And who decided.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to share a big plan that ended up small.
english: The Segway was supposed to change how cities work.
Now it's mostly just tours.
I have big plans that end small too.
Still counts, though.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine a pineapple as the star of the party.
english: Pineapples used to be so expensive people rented them.
Not to eat. Just to show off.
Imagine a pineapple just sitting there at the party.
Famous. Untouched.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to how loud that would be.
english: The loudest burp ever was louder than a lawnmower.
A whole lawnmower.
I need to hear that.
From a safe distance.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess what happened to that person.
english: In Alaska, you can't wake a sleeping bear just for a photo.
It's an actual law.
Which means someone definitely tried it.
I have questions for that person.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to go tell someone the word "tittle."
english: The dot above "i" and "j" has its own name.
It's called a tittle.
Tiny thing. Real name.
Now you know something almost nobody else does.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to agree or disagree that spite worked out here.
english: Potato crisps exist because someone complained.
Said the fries were too thick.
So the chef sliced them stupidly thin out of spite.
Best decision anyone's ever made out of spite.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what they use that tiny pocket for.
english: That tiny pocket on jeans was made for a pocket watch.
Nobody carries pocket watches anymore.
I've never once used mine for anything.
It just exists. Doing nothing.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine how they'd keep track of time up there.
english: Astronauts on the Space Station see about 16 sunrises a day.
Sixteen. Every single day.
I don't know when I'd ever decide to sleep.
Or eat breakfast, honestly.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to the timeline being scrambled.
english: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire.
That completely broke my sense of time.
I thought I knew which things were old.
Apparently not.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to nature's unnecessary creativity.
english: Wombats make cube-shaped poop.
Actual cubes.
Nature didn't have to do that.
But it did.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to plan their snack and nap strategy.
english: The longest film ever made lasts more than 35 days.
Thirty-five days. Of just watching.
I'd need so many snacks.
And several naps.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess why anyone would print money nobody can use.
english: The largest banknote ever made was worth 100,000 dollars.
Nobody ever actually used it to buy anything.
What's the point of money you can't spend.
I have so many questions about that meeting.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to notice their own body doing something pointless out of habit.
english: Goosebumps used to fluff up ancestors' fur.
To make them look bigger.
I don't have fur, but my skin still tries.
Bless it, honestly.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess how anyone counted that many lakes.
english: Canada has more lakes than every other country combined.
Combined. All of them.
I wonder who had to count them all.
Bet they stopped believing in lakes.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to decide whether white chocolate counts as chocolate.
english: White chocolate has no actual cocoa in it.
None at all.
So is it even chocolate?
I have opinions, and they are strong.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine having that job.
english: The first traffic lights used gas lamps.
Someone had to light them. By hand.
Imagine that job.
Hope they weren't running late.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to admit whether they just yawned.
english: Yawning is contagious.
Even just thinking about it can make you yawn.
I said "yawn" and now I'm yawning.
See what you just did.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what they thought a violin was made of.
english: A violin is made from more than 70 pieces of wood.
Seventy. For something that small.
I thought it was basically one block with strings.
I was very wrong.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess what rank the bear might have had.
english: A bear named Wojtek was an official member of the Polish Army.
He carried ammunition boxes.
An actual bear. An actual job.
I wonder what his rank was.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to what ancient priorities were.
english: The oldest known recipe in the world isn't for bread.
It's for beer.
Ancient people had their priorities sorted.
Respect.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what they would hold on to.
english: Sea otters hold hands while they sleep.
So they don't drift away from each other.
I think I'd hold on to something silly.
Like a spoon.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to a building that stretches.
english: The Eiffel Tower gets slightly taller in summer.
The heat makes the metal expand.
Like it's stretching.
Mood.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to how close a call that is.
english: Your stomach grows a new lining every few days.
So it doesn't digest itself.
Which means it almost does, constantly.
Cutting it close, honestly.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to how unbothered the sky is about this.
english: Lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Five times hotter. For a second.
And it just happens. In the sky. Casually.
Nothing about that feels casual to me.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to try picturing the comparison.
english: Australia is wider than the Moon.
A whole country. Wider than a whole moon.
I don't know how to picture that.
My brain just gave up.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what annoyance they'd turn into an invention.
english: Velcro was invented because of burrs stuck to a dog's fur.
Someone actually looked closely at them.
Most people would've just been annoyed.
He made a fortune instead.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what gift they'd want.
english: Penguins give each other stones as gifts.
Smooth ones. Chosen carefully.
That might be the sweetest thing I've heard all day.
I'd want a really good stone.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to the scale of that.
english: There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth.
Every beach. All the sand.
And there's still more stars than that.
I need to sit down.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to the peanut's true identity.
english: Peanuts aren't actually nuts.
They're legumes. Like beans.
This changes nothing about how I eat them.
But I feel deceived.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine carrying that phone.
english: The first mobile phone call was made in 1973.
On a phone that weighed over a kilogram.
Imagine that in your pocket.
You'd need a second pocket just for balance.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what animal ability they'd want.
english: A giraffe can clean its own ears with its tongue.
Its actual tongue.
That would save me so much time.
I'm a little jealous, honestly.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to noticing it for the first time.
english: The Mona Lisa doesn't have eyebrows.
Removing them used to be fashionable.
I stared at that painting for years and never noticed.
Now I can't unsee it.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to go tell someone what "robot" really means.
english: The word "robot" comes from a Czech word.
It means "forced work."
Every robot's name is basically a tiny complaint.
Now you can tell someone that.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to think of their own embarrassing smell memory.
english: Your nose can remember thousands of different smells.
Thousands.
Mine's definitely holding onto some embarrassing ones.
I'm not going to say which.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say whether they'd have the patience to watch.
english: Giant bamboo can grow almost a metre in a single day.
One day.
You could watch it grow if you had the patience.
I do not have the patience.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine that investigation.
english: Koala fingerprints look almost exactly like human ones.
Close enough to confuse investigators.
Imagine being a detective and a koala's the suspect.
Case closed, apparently.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what event they'd have entered.
english: The Olympics used to include competitions for painting and poetry.
Actual medals for actual poems.
I wonder what event I'd have entered.
Probably napping. Competitively.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say whether they'd want to live there.
english: Iceland has no native snakes at all.
None. Ever.
I think I'd move there just for that.
Snakes can keep their distance.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to notice something small doing its job unnoticed.
english: Those little metal rivets on jeans stop the pockets from tearing.
I never once wondered what those were for.
They've just been quietly doing their job.
The whole time.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to help make Félicette more famous.
english: In 1963, a cat named Félicette went to space.
The first cat ever.
I'd never heard her name before today.
She deserves way more credit.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to decide whether a cucumber really counts as food.
english: Cucumbers are about 95% water.
Basically just water with a shape.
I'm not sure that counts as a vegetable.
It's giving its best, though.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to the tower's stubbornness.
english: The Leaning Tower of Pisa has been leaning for over 800 years.
Never once fallen.
That's just pure stubbornness at this point.
I admire it.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to try it themselves.
english: You can't tickle yourself.
Your brain already knows it's coming.
I just tried. Nothing.
Deeply unfair, honestly.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what they'd want to do standing next to it.
english: The tallest tree in the world is taller than a football pitch is long.
If you laid it down, it wouldn't even fit.
That's an enormous tree.
I want to stand next to it.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to share their own happy accident.
english: The Slinky was invented by accident.
An engineer just knocked a spring off a shelf.
And watched it walk.
Best mistake in toy history.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to share their own quick-thinking moment.
english: Ice cream cones became popular after a seller ran out of bowls.
He borrowed rolled waffles from the stall next door.
Under pressure. On the spot.
That's the kind of thinking I respect.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess what other birds do differently.
english: Puffins build their nests underground.
Not up in a tree. Underground.
That's not what I expect from a bird.
Puffins do their own thing.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess what those old photos looked like.
english: The first digital camera had a resolution of just 0.01 megapixels.
Black and white. Barely there.
I can't imagine what those photos even looked like.
Probably just... blobs.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to the tomato's long-overdue innocence.
english: People used to think tomatoes were dangerous to eat.
Turns out it wasn't the tomato. It was the lead in the plates.
Poor tomato took the blame for centuries.
Completely innocent, it turns out.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess or invent a snow word of their own.
english: Scotland has more than 400 words for snow.
Four hundred different kinds.
I only really know "cold" and "very cold."
I have a lot to learn.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to their body doing this without asking.
english: Babies have more bones than adults.
Some of them join together as you grow.
Your body's been quietly merging bones this whole time.
Didn't even ask permission.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to go use the word "pandemonium."
english: A group of parrots is called a pandemonium.
That's the actual name.
Somehow, it fits perfectly.
Now you know a new word to use.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine riding one uphill.
english: The first bicycles had no pedals.
You just pushed with your feet.
Imagine trying to go uphill like that.
Absolutely not.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to something that sounds fake but is real.
english: Sometimes it rains fish.
Storms lift them out of shallow water and drop them somewhere else.
That sounds completely made up.
It isn't.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to count a piano's keys themselves.
english: A piano has 88 keys.
Some special ones have even more.
I've never once counted them myself.
Now I really want to.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to try turning their own head that far.
english: Sloths can turn their heads about 270 degrees.
Almost all the way around.
I tried it just now.
My neck said no.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to try picturing that weight.
english: One teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh about a billion tonnes.
A teaspoon. A billion tonnes.
I can't even picture that.
My brain just refuses.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine trying it themselves.
english: The first rubber erasers were made from pieces of bread.
People used to rub out pencil marks with bread.
I need to try that at least once.
For research.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to share an unfinished thought of their own.
english: People remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones.
Your brain just won't let them go.
That explains a lot about me, actually.
I have several unfinished thoughts right now.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what "shovels" they'd sell instead of digging.
english: During the Gold Rush, some people got richer selling shovels than finding gold.
Not glamorous. Just useful.
I respect the boring hustle.
Selling shovels while everyone else digs.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to declare their own snack as medicine.
english: Lollipops used to be sold as throat medicine.
An actual excuse to eat candy.
I'm calling all my snacks medicine from now on.
It's basically true.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to the cloud's deception.
english: A single cloud can weigh more than 500 elephants.
Five hundred elephants. Just floating there.
It looks so light, though.
Total liar, that cloud.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to check their own hands.
english: Your fingernails grow faster on your dominant hand.
The one you use more.
I'm checking mine right now.
Yep. Faster.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to that leap of imagination.
english: Play-Doh was originally made to clean wallpaper.
Not to play with. To clean.
Somebody looked at cleaning goo and saw a toy.
Vision, honestly.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to share something they do just for fun.
english: Ravens have been seen sliding down snowy roofs.
Just for fun. No reason.
That might be the most relatable bird behaviour I've heard.
Same, honestly.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say how they'd have passed the time.
english: The longest traffic jam ever was about 100 kilometres long.
A hundred kilometres of just sitting there.
I'd have made so many friends with the other cars.
Or fallen asleep. One of the two.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to compare their own track record to Roman concrete.
english: The ancient Romans made concrete from volcanic ash.
Some of it is still standing today.
That's built to outlast literally everyone.
I can't even keep a plant alive.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine seeing that themselves.
english: If you put Saturn in a big enough ocean, it would float.
An entire planet. Floating.
I need to see that.
Someone build the ocean.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to how clever that plan is.
english: Crows have been seen using traffic lights to crack nuts.
They drop them, let the cars run them over, then wait for the red light to collect them.
That's an actual plan.
Smarter than me most mornings.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to carrots' true original colour.
english: Carrots used to be purple.
Orange ones came much later.
I've been eating the wrong colour this whole time.
Someone owes purple carrots an apology.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to go visit it themselves.
english: The first website ever made is still online today.
You can visit it right now.
It's just sitting there, exactly as it started.
I want to go say hello to it.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to guess how people there keep track of time.
english: There's a town in Norway where the Sun doesn't rise for part of winter.
Weeks of just... darkness.
I wonder how they know when to wake up.
Probably just guessing, like the rest of us.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what feels uniquely theirs.
english: Identical twins don't have the same fingerprints.
Not even close ones.
Everyone gets to keep at least one thing that's only theirs.
I like that.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to think of something else that's lasted that long.
english: LEGO bricks made today still fit bricks made 60 years ago.
Perfectly. Every time.
Nothing else I own has lasted that consistently.
Not even close.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine seeing that themselves.
english: Some waterfalls appear to flow backwards in strong wind.
The water just gets pushed back up.
I need to see that in person.
Immediately.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to react to that image.
english: Goats have rectangular pupils.
Not round ones. Rectangles.
I looked it up just to be sure.
It's true. And a little unsettling.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to say what they'd pay taxes with.
english: People once paid their taxes with giant wheels of cheese.
Actual cheese. As payment.
I'd pay taxes so much faster like that.
Bring it back.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to imagine what the tree might have "seen."
english: The world's oldest living tree started growing before the pyramids were built.
Before the pyramids.
It's just been standing there this whole time.
Watching everything happen.

conversationGoal: Invite the child to admit whether they do this too.
english: People are much more likely to sing when they think nobody's listening.
Completely different when no one's around.
I do this constantly.
Don't ask about the sound.
